newsitem.title: USA: Document accuses Swiss of aiding Nazi war effort.
newsitem.headline: Document accuses Swiss of aiding Nazi war effort.

text.p: The Allies were so outraged at massive Swiss supplies of munitions to Germany during the Second World War that they considered mounting an economic boycott of the neutral country, according to U.S. government documents released on Thursday by a Jewish group.

Among the documents was an October 1943 letter in which the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, Adm. William Leahy, told Secretary of State Cordell Hull that Swiss munitions supplies to Germany were "materially decreasing the military effectiveness of our air attacks on the Axis."

Leahy was worried because the Swiss were increasing munitions supplies "at the very time that the British and American combined bomber offensive is beginning to substantially affect German production of munitions."

He added, "It is the opinion of the Joints Chiefs of Staff that Switzerland should not be permitted to receive any imports whatsoever which we can control so long as she continues to lend material aid to the German war effort."

The letter and other documents were released by the World Jewish Congress, which has been combing the National Archives to trace Swiss actions during the war in a dispute with Switzerland on whether its banks still held funds deposited by Holocaust victims. WJC Vice President Kalman Sultanik said the new documents "demonstrate that Swiss aid to the Nazis lengthened the war and cost precious American blood."

A spokesman for the Swiss Embassy in Washington said he could not comment on documents he had not seen but that much of the archive material now being unearthed has been known by scholars for many years.
Columbia University historian James Shenton, an expert on the Second World War, said he was not aware of the Leahy letter but that the admiral was a strong critic of the Swiss.

It has long been known that Switzerland and Sweden, both neutrals, aided the German war effort, with the Swedes providing the Reich with such vital minerals as iron ore and the Swiss providing financial services and manufactured goods, including machine tools, ball bearings, electrical equipment, small arms and ammunition.

Shenton said there was not much the Allies could do to stop Swiss supplies other than pressure the nation, which was entirely surrounded by Germany and countries under German control. But there were about 40 "accidental" bombings of Swiss territory by the Allies during the war that Shenton said may have been meant as reminders of Allied concern.

In his letter to Hull, Leahy said the most effective way of stopping the supplies would be to cut off Switzerland's access to financial and "in transit" facilities, by denying it the right to buy materials in territories controlled by the allies and "by the exercise of the legal right of blockade."
